messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 26
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Firefighter
- Trauma Type: Captivity
- Pcl5: 45

At 26, she has already built a life around running toward danger. As a firefighter, she is used to heat, noise, and the sharp discipline of emergencies. She likes the clarity of the work: the radio crackles, someone gives an order, and her body knows what to do. Before the trauma, she thinks of herself as capable and steady, the one in her crew who can keep moving when everyone else is overwhelmed.

The event begins on what is supposed to be a routine response. Her unit is called to a fire in a deteriorating industrial building on the edge of town. Inside, conditions shift quickly. Smoke thickens, visibility drops, and part of the structure gives way. In the confusion, she becomes separated from the rest of her crew. She calls out over the radio, but the signal is broken and full of static. She tries to follow the wall toward an exit and instead ends up trapped behind a collapsed section of debris in a small concrete service room.

At first she tells herself it is temporary. She has training for this. Someone will notice she is missing. But the air is hot and stale, and the darkness feels total except for the weak beam of her flashlight. Time stops making sense. She conserves her oxygen, bangs on the wall, listens for voices, hears nothing, then hears sounds she cannot trust. She becomes aware of every bodily sensation—the tightening in her chest, the sweat cooling on her back, the pounding in her throat. She starts thinking in fragments: not here, not like this, stay awake, keep breathing. At some point her flashlight dies. The loss of that small circle of light feels worse than the collapse itself. She later says the worst part is not only the fear that she will die, but the feeling of being cut off from the world, buried alive and unreachable.

She is found alive several hours later. By then she is dehydrated, coughing, and barely able to orient herself when rescuers pull her free. In the hospital, people tell her she is lucky. Her crew visits. Her captain squeezes her shoulder and jokes in the familiar way of the station, trying to make things normal again. She laughs because that is easier than explaining that when she closes her eyes she is still in the dark room, counting breaths.

In the first weeks afterward, she tries to return to work too quickly. She tells herself that getting back on the truck will prove she is fine. Instead, she begins to unravel in quiet, private ways. At the station, the smell of smoke on turnout gear turns her stomach. During drills, if she has to enter a narrow training space, her thoughts race and her hands shake inside her gloves. She becomes intensely aware of exits and starts positioning herself near doors without meaning to. When a bay door sticks one morning and the engine noise echoes too loudly, she feels a surge of panic so strong that she has to step outside and pretend she is taking a phone call.

Sleep becomes fractured. She dreads going to bed because the same images return: blackness, pressure, the dead flashlight, the certainty that no one is coming. On some nights she wakes disoriented and clawing at her sheets, convinced for a moment that debris is pinning her down. She starts leaving lights on in her apartment, then feels embarrassed by it, as if she has become childish. She used to enjoy living alone; now the silence feels hostile. She keeps the television on for background noise and checks the locks repeatedly before bed.

Her world gets smaller without her planning it. She avoids elevators, underground parking garages, and crowded bars where she might feel hemmed in. Friends invite her out after shifts, but she often declines, saying she is tired. It is partly true. She is exhausted all the time, worn down by poor sleep and by the effort of appearing normal. When she does go out, she scans the room automatically, notices blocked exits, flinches if someone comes up behind her. She has become irritable in ways that surprise her. At work, she snaps at a newer firefighter for hesitating during a drill, then feels ashamed because she knows the reaction is out of proportion.

What troubles her most is the change in how she sees herself. She had always believed that courage meant control under pressure. Now she worries that something essential in her has been altered. She replays the event and interrogates her own actions—whether she turned the wrong way, whether she should have stayed calmer, whether she somehow failed her crew by needing to be rescued. She knows, rationally, that buildings collapse and people get trapped. But her body does not respond to reason. Every siren primes her. Every confined space becomes a test.

Months later, she is still showing up for shifts, still pulling on her gear, still doing the work she once loved without thinking. From the outside she appears functional, even tough. But inside she is braced all the time, as if another wall might give way at any moment. The world no longer feels reliably open. It feels narrow, unstable, and one blocked exit away from darkness.
